passage:
"Harish, helmet!" Parul held it out at the gate.
"Didi, it's two minutes on the cycle to tuition."
"Two minutes is enough."
"It squashes my hair. Nobody wears one for short rides."
"Remember Sunny from B-block? Short ride too."
"Sunny was showing off. I ride properly."
"And the auto that took the turn without looking? Was Sunny showing off then?"
"Didi, relax. Nothing's going to happen to me."
"That's exactly what Sunny said."
Harish grinned and pushed off the kerb. "I'm different."
Parul didn't smile. She stood in front of the cycle, holding the helmet out, until he sighed, snatched it and jammed it on.

qa.q: Why does Harish say he doesn't need the helmet?
qa.a: He says it's two minutes on the cycle to tuition and the helmet squashes his hair.

qa.q: Why does Harish feel that nothing is going to happen to him?
qa.a: He tells himself Sunny was showing off and he rides properly, so harm feels like it belongs to others, while the comfort of no helmet is right now.

qa.q: Which of Parul's moves worked, and why?
qa.a: Standing calmly in front of the cycle worked better than more arguing, because it kept the choice in front of him and let him give in without a fight.

qa.q: What is it like for Parul to watch Harish push off without a helmet?
qa.a: Parul remembers what happened to Sunny, so she feels a real fear that he doesn't, which is why she didn't smile.

grounding: A teenager insists he won't get hurt riding without a helmet, seeing accidents as something for other riders.

passage: I'm Amandeep, and I'm writing this a few months after the thing with Jatin's vape. It started in Class 10, behind the school water tank. Jatin had a flavoured one, mango, and passed it around. I knew the posters in the corridor said it was harmful. But in my head those posters were about other people, adults who'd smoked for twenty years, not a sixteen-year-old taking a few puffs. The sweet taste and everyone laughing felt huge right then; 'later' felt like a made-up word. Within weeks Jatin was sneaking out between classes, and irritable when he couldn't. That scared me more than any poster. I stopped going to the water tank, and I told my older cousin, who helped Jatin talk to the school counsellor.

qa.q: Where did it start?
qa.a: It started in Class 10, behind the school water tank.

qa.q: Why didn't the corridor posters feel like they applied to Amandeep?
qa.a: Amandeep felt safe, thinking the posters were about other people who had smoked for years, and the sweet taste and laughter right then felt much bigger than 'later'.

qa.q: What did Amandeep do that was wise?
qa.a: Amandeep stepped away from the water tank and told an older cousin, who helped Jatin reach the school counsellor.

qa.q: How did Jatin's changes affect Amandeep?
qa.a: Seeing Jatin sneak out between classes and turn irritable scared Amandeep more than any poster, and made the harm real.

grounding: A teenager recalls believing vaping harms only other people, while the immediate buzz outweighed any thought of later.

passage:
Note from Coach Trisha, district swimming camp, day 4
This afternoon Ojas and two older boys slipped away to the old quarry pond behind the camp. There's a board there saying the water is deep and cold. When I found them, Ojas was on the ledge, ready to jump. He said, laughing, "Coach, I'm the strongest swimmer here. Those warnings are for people who can't swim." He seemed to truly believe it. The rush of the jump was all he could see.
I didn't shout. I sat with him on the bank and asked who he thought the board was written for. He shrugged. I told him strong swimmers get cramps in cold water too.
Next steps: told the camp head and called his parents this evening. Tomorrow the whole group walks to the quarry with the lifeguard to hear about the risks on site.

qa.q: What does the board at the quarry pond say?
qa.a: The board says the water is deep and cold.

qa.q: What does Ojas's laughing reply suggest about how he sees the danger?
qa.a: It suggests Ojas feels confident, even thrilled, truly believing the warning is for weaker swimmers, while the rush of the jump outweighs any thought of harm.

qa.q: How did Coach Trisha respond without lecturing?
qa.a: Coach Trisha sat with him, asked who the board was for, told the camp head and his parents the same day, and planned a site visit with the lifeguard.

qa.q: How might Ojas's parents feel when they hear about the quarry?
qa.a: They would likely feel scared, and grateful the coach found him in time.

grounding: A coach records a strong teenage swimmer believing a danger sign is only for weaker people, and the calm steps taken.

passage:
14 Aug
Went to the fair with Rajni didi and her cousin. On the way back I rode pillion on his scooter, no helmet because it was in the dickey and I didn't want to wait. The wind in my face at night, the lights on the canal road, honestly the BEST feeling.
Rajni didi said, "Jasleen, put the helmet on, silly girl." Please. Accidents happen to careless people who ride fast in traffic. We were only on the canal road, and her cousin drives well.
Also, everyone in my class says their brothers ride without one. Nothing ever happens to them.
When we reached home Rajni didi was really quiet. She told me her college friend fell off a scooter last year on a road just like that one. She didn't say more.
I still don't think it would happen to me. But I keep hearing how quiet she was.
Jasleen

qa.q: Where was the helmet when Jasleen rode pillion?
qa.a: It was in the dickey.

qa.q: Why did riding without a helmet feel safe to Jasleen?
qa.a: The wind and lights felt so good in the moment, and she believed accidents happen only to careless people riding fast in traffic, not to her on the canal road.

qa.q: What could Rajni didi try next time to help Jasleen choose the helmet?
qa.a: She could ask Jasleen to wait the few seconds and hand her the helmet before they start, and talk calmly about her friend so it doesn't feel like a scolding.

qa.q: What is it like for Rajni didi to hear Jasleen shrug off the helmet?
qa.a: For Rajni didi it may bring back the fear of her college friend's fall, which is why she went quiet instead of arguing.

grounding: A teenager's diary shows her riding without a helmet, believing harm happens to others, drawn by the thrill of the ride in the moment.

passage:
Arnab: so I tried the vape at Dev's party
Kalyani: wait what
Arnab: relax. it's literally mango flavoured air
Kalyani: it's not air
Arnab: people who get hooked are weak. I just tried it once, I can stop anytime
Kalyani: that's what everyone says
Arnab: ya but I'm not everyone. I play football, my lungs are fine
Kalyani: dev's brother said the same last year. now he can't go a day
Arnab: dev's brother is different
Kalyani: how
Arnab: he just is
Arnab: it felt really good though. like the whole room slowed down
Kalyani: that's the part that worries me
Kalyani: if it starts pulling at you, will you talk to your mum or the counsellor? not a lecture. just someone
Arnab: it won't come to that
Arnab: ...ok fine. if it does

qa.q: What flavour did Arnab say the vape was?
qa.a: Arnab said it was mango flavoured.

qa.q: Why does Arnab feel so sure the vape won't be a problem?
qa.a: The good feeling in the moment was strong, and Arnab trusts being a fit football player who can stop anytime, so getting hooked seems like something that happens only to weaker people.

qa.q: What small step did Kalyani ask Arnab to agree to?
qa.a: Kalyani asked Arnab to talk to a mum or the counsellor if it ever starts pulling, and Arnab finally agreed.

qa.q: What worries Kalyani most about what Arnab said?
qa.a: The part where the whole room slowed down worries Kalyani, because it shows how rewarding it felt, and Kalyani has seen Dev's brother get hooked after saying the same things.

grounding: A chat shows a teenager who tried vaping believing harm is for others, pulled by the immediate good feeling, while a friend gently points Arnab to a trusted adult.
